subtopic: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
explanation: Inheritance lets a derived class reuse the data members and member functions already written in its base class, which is the textbook mechanism for reusability in OOP. Encapsulation and abstraction control visibility and detail-hiding, and polymorphism gives one interface many behaviours, but none of them reuse existing code.

subtopic: Constructors and destructors
explanation: Passing by reference binds the parameter to the caller's existing object instead of constructing a copy, so no extra object is created and therefore no destructor runs when the function returns. The trap is option (a), which is what happens on pass by value, where the copy's destructor fires at end of function.
note: The stem is loose: the original object is of course still destroyed later in the caller's scope; the intended point is that the reference parameter itself causes no destructor call.

subtopic: Inheritance, virtual functions and pointers to objects
explanation: A class containing at least one pure virtual function is abstract, and the compiler forbids instantiating it because part of its interface has no implementation; it can only be used through pointers or references to derived objects. Parent, anonymous and nested classes are all ordinary instantiable classes.
note: Option (b) carries a stray OCR character ('Abstract class !'); the wording is otherwise intact and the question is answerable.

subtopic: Exception handling and strings
explanation: Several catch handlers on one try block are optional and can be collapsed into a single handler, either catch(...) or a handler taking a common base-class exception, so option (b) is the only true statement. Options (a), (c) and (d) all assert the opposite of the rule that one try block may have one or many catch blocks.

subtopic: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
explanation: Standard OOP texts pair the two directly: polymorphism, letting objects at different levels of a hierarchy share one external interface, is what makes an inheritance hierarchy useful, and is described as being extensively used in implementing inheritance. Dynamic binding is the run-time mechanism polymorphism relies on rather than the feature itself, and operator overloading is only one narrow form of polymorphism.
note: Dynamic binding is a defensible second reading, since virtual dispatch is how a compiler actually implements the inheritance hierarchy.

subtopic: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
explanation: Dynamic objects are allocated with new and destroyed with delete at points the programmer chooses, so they exist only for a particular period decided at run time; static and external objects instead survive for the whole program run. Automatic objects are the near miss, but their period is fixed by block entry and exit rather than being a chosen one.
note: The blank naming the object type was lost in the scan, and 'exists for a particular period' could also be read as describing an automatic object.

subtopic: Classes, objects, member functions and memory allocation
explanation: A static object declared inside a function is visible only within that block, exactly like an automatic object, but it is created once and lives until the program ends, exactly like an external object. Automatic objects fail the lifetime half of the definition and external objects fail the scope half.
note: The blank before 'object' was lost in the scan, so the stem reads 'A object is an object which...'.

subtopic: Constructors and destructors
explanation: Constructors cannot be declared virtual: the virtual mechanism needs an already-constructed object whose vtable pointer is set, and the exact type is known statically at the point of construction anyway, so option (a) is the non-characteristic. The classic trap is that destructors can and often should be virtual, while the other three statements are genuine constructor properties, including the fact that a constructor has no address you can take.

subtopic: OOP concepts, applications and the OOP process
explanation: Dynamic (late) binding means the code executed for a call is chosen at run time from the actual object's type, which requires both an inheritance hierarchy and a polymorphic virtual interface; that is the standard textbook sentence this stem is taken from. Message passing, abstraction and encapsulation are separate concepts and none of them depend on run-time type resolution.

subtopic: Entity-Relationship modelling
explanation: In ER modelling an attribute is precisely the property that describes a characteristic of an entity, such as name or date of birth. 'Column' is the tempting distractor but it is the physical relational-table term for where an attribute is stored, not the ER concept.

subtopic: Data models and the relational model: keys, tuples, domains and relational algebra
explanation: The hierarchical model organises records as a tree of parent-child links, where every child segment has exactly one parent. The network model is the near miss: it generalises the same idea to a graph so a child may have several parents, which is why it is not a tree.

subtopic: SQL and basic query statements
explanation: ORDER BY is the clause that sorts the result set on one or more columns, ASC by default and DESC when asked. GROUP BY aggregates rows rather than sorting them, and HAVING filters those groups.

subtopic: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
explanation: 5NF, also called project-join normal form, removes join dependencies: a relation is in 5NF when every non-trivial join dependency is implied by its candidate keys, so it cannot be losslessly decomposed further. Multivalued dependency is the classic trap here because that is what 4NF addresses, and plain functional dependency belongs to 2NF/3NF/BCNF.

subtopic: Concurrency control, locking and time stamping
explanation: A cycle of transactions each waiting for a data item locked by another is the definition of a deadlock, and no transaction in the cycle can ever proceed without intervention. The other three terms are not standard DBMS concurrency terminology.

subtopic: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
explanation: Normalization is exactly the process of decomposing schemas, guided by functional dependencies, so that information is stored without unnecessary redundancy and the update, insert and delete anomalies redundancy causes disappear. Assertions and integrity constraints police correctness rather than redundancy.

subtopic: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
explanation: X to Y means each X value determines exactly one Y value, and Y to X means each Y value determines exactly one X value; holding both directions at once makes the mapping a bijection, that is 1:1. If only X to Y held, the relationship would be many-to-one.
note: The '>' characters in the stem are OCR for the functional-dependency arrow.

subtopic: Query processing and optimisation
explanation: Among the standard equivalence rules, selection distributes over all three set operations, union, intersection and set difference, because a selection is a row-wise predicate and applying it before or after the set operation yields the same tuples. Projection, by contrast, distributes only over union, which is the distinction this question is testing.

subtopic: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
explanation: 2NF requires that no non-prime attribute be functionally dependent on only part of a composite candidate key, that is, no partial functional dependencies exist. Option (b) is the giveaway trap: functional dependencies certainly do still exist in 2NF, and multivalued dependencies are the concern of 4NF, not 2NF.

subtopic: Entity-Relationship modelling
explanation: Total participation, meaning every entity in the set must take part in the relationship, is drawn as a double line between the entity rectangle and the relationship diamond. A single line denotes partial participation, and dashed lines are used for linking attributes to relationships.

explanation: Only timestamp ordering satisfies both requirements: it produces conflict-serializable schedules and it never makes a transaction wait, aborting and restarting the offender instead, so a deadlock cycle cannot form. Two-phase locking guarantees conflict serializability but transactions do wait on locks, so 2PL can deadlock; hence statement I only. subtopic: Transaction processing, schedules and recoverability
explanation: Enforcing atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability requires logging, locking and recovery machinery, so ACID adds complexity to a system rather than decreasing it, making that the false statement. The other three are true: ACID does cost performance, does keep data consistent, and is what allows many concurrent transactions to be managed safely.

subtopic: Database design, functional dependencies and normal forms
explanation: Reducing redundancy is the core design guideline, because duplicated data is what produces insertion, update and deletion anomalies. The other three options each invert a rule of good design: a design must be unambiguous, unrelated data belongs in separate tables, and entities are described precisely by their attributes.

subtopic: Query processing and optimisation
explanation: Query optimization is by definition the step that chooses a good, low-cost evaluation plan among the many equivalent ones for a query. Query processing is the wider pipeline of parsing, optimizing and executing, of which optimization is only one phase.

subtopic: Data models and the relational model: keys, tuples, domains and relational algebra
explanation: Standard texts introduce tuple relational calculus first, with variables ranging over tuples, and then present domain relational calculus, whose variables range over attribute domains, as the second form. So the 'second form' being named here is the domain relational calculus; 'attribute relational calculus' is not a real term.
note: The stem does not say which form was the first, so the answer relies on the usual textbook order in which tuple calculus is presented before domain calculus.

subtopic: Database system concepts, architecture, interfaces and data independence
explanation: The two files the DBMS itself maintains and consults while running are the data dictionary, holding metadata about schemas, users and privileges, and the transaction log, recording every change so failures can be recovered from. The distractors all name languages or tools, and a query language is not a file.
note: Loosely worded textbook question; 'two files' is really shorthand for the metadata catalogue and the log.
